## A Government Can Kill by Abandonment
We have been trained to recognize state violence primarily when it takes the form of a weapon, a prison cell, a deportation van, or a uniformed officer.
Those forms are real, terribly real, and the administration's campaign of raids, detention, xenophobia, racial targeting, and expulsion deserves its own full accounting.
But governments also harm through _subtraction_.
They withdraw medication. Food. Income. The doctor. The home-care worker. The case manager. The legal protection that kept a person in their community.
They withdraw the public institution that once answered the phone, processed the claim, investigated the abuse, or enforced the right.
**Then they point to the ruined person and call the ruin evidence of personal failure.**
This is why the "kill line" is more than a viral phrase. It reveals the connective tissue among policies usually discussed separately.
SNAP cuts are not merely agricultural policy.
Medicaid cuts are not merely health policy.
The SSI asset ceiling is not merely an outdated technical limit.
Housing scarcity is not merely a local zoning problem.
Weakening _Olmstead_ enforcement is not merely a disagreement among lawyers.
Together, they determine whether a human being has enough margin to survive a shock, whether they can accumulate the resources to recover, whether they remain connected to a community, and whether the state recognizes an obligation to help them return.
**That is the line between a society and a sorting mechanism.**
A functioning civilization does not guarantee that no one will ever fall. Illness, grief, disability, addiction, economic disruption, and bad decisions will always exist.
Its moral test is whether falling behind becomes a permanent sentence.
Can a person get sick without losing their home?
Can a disabled person save enough to survive a broken transmission in their car?
Can a mother leave an abusive household without becoming homeless?
Can a worker lose a job without losing healthcare?
Can an elderly person receive care in the home they have lived in for fifty years?
Can a person experience addiction or mental illness and still be treated as someone whose life has a future?
Can someone make a mistake and remain a member of society?
The answer being constructed by this government is increasingly: o**nly if the market still finds you useful, your family can privately absorb the cost, or you possess enough wealth to purchase your own mercy.**
For everyone else, the margin is being narrowed.
The floor is being lowered.
The ladder back up is being pulled away.
We do not need to invent a conspiracy to see what is happening. We need only follow the appropriations, eligibility rules, legal opinions, price data, coverage losses, and human consequences to their _shared destination._
America's kill line is not merely an economic condition anymore.
**It is becoming an instrument of governance.**
And the first obligation of anyone seeking power in this moment is to say so--before millions more people are pushed across it and blamed for the fall.
Care. Courage. The Constitution.

America is not merely failing to catch people when they fall. Its government is actively removing the ground beneath them--and weakening the routes by which they might ever return. | | | Jul 27 | | | | | | | | | | | | Watch a 4:30 video summarizing this article, above. There is a phrase circulating internationally for a condition Americans know intimately, even when they have never had a name for it: the "kill line." The kill line is the invisible financial threshold beyond which a person can no longer absorb an ordinary shock. Above it, a car repair is an expense. Below it, the same repair means you cannot get to work. Losing wages means you cannot pay rent. Missing rent damages your credit or begins an eviction. Bad credit makes the next apartment, car, or emergency loan more expensive or unavailable. One disruption becomes five, and then ten, because every system you encounter begins penalizing you for having been hurt by the system before it. For tens of millions of Americans, financial stability no longer means having savings, security, or a plausible route into a better life. It means remaining current on a stack of obligations for one more month. Their income does not build wealth. It feeds rent, debt, premiums, deductibles, utilities, childcare, transportation, and groceries. Every dollar is already assigned before it arrives. The phrase "paycheck to paycheck" does not quite capture this. It sounds like a budgeting problem or a temporary shortage. The kill line is structural. It means there is no fault tolerance left in a person's life. One illness, one firing, one abusive landlord, one bureaucratic mistake, one insurance denial, one family emergency, one accident, and the architecture of ordinary life begins collapsing around them. What makes the present moment so dangerous is that the federal government is not merely declining to solve this condition. It is actively adopting policies that push more people toward and across that line. It is taking food, healthcare, administrative access, and community-based support away from people who already have almost no margin. It is preserving or expanding systems that prevent disabled and elderly people from accumulating even a modest reserve. And now it is advancing a legal theory that would weaken the federal government's responsibility to prevent disabled people from being unnecessarily confined in institutions. No single one of these decisions proves a secret extermination plan. Governments almost never write their most morally repellent purposes into a single document. Policy is fragmented across statutes, agency rules, budget tables, eligibility reviews, legal memoranda, administrative burdens, funding formulas, and judicial arguments. But we are not required to ignore a pattern merely because it has been divided into departments. When a government knows that millions of people are living one emergency from ruin, takes away their food and healthcare, restricts their ability to save, makes survival more expensive, and weakens their legal right to remain in their own communities - all while empowering corporations and billionaires to exploit the public - we should describe the cumulative result honestly. This is not just austerity. It is the construction of a write-off society. First, Remove the Margin The central mechanism of the kill line is the elimination of margin. You do not have to make everyone destitute at once. You only have to reduce the number of people capable of surviving the next shock. The 2025 reconciliation law did precisely that across several of the country's largest social programs. According to the Congressional Budget Office, its Medicaid changes are projected to reduce Medicaid enrollment by roughly 13 million people by 2035. CBO estimates that the law will increase the number of uninsured people by 7.5 million through 2034 through its Medicaid provisions alone. The same law is projected to reduce federal SNAP spending by more than $200 billion through 2035 by cutting participation, reducing average benefits, expanding work requirements, changing eligibility, and shifting costs onto states. While pouring over a trillion dollars per year into privatized, profitable war and violence all over the globe. Why is there money for bombs and billionaires, but not bread and butter? The effects are not merely projections awaiting some distant year. One analysis published a year after the legislation's enactment found that SNAP participation had already fallen by more than 4 million people and Affordable Care Act plan selections by 1.2 million. That is what pushing people toward the kill line looks like in administrative language. A family loses food assistance. Its hunger does not appear in the federal budget as hunger. It appears as "reduced outlays." A patient loses Medicaid. Their untreated illness does not appear as an injury inflicted by the legislation. It appears as "lower enrollment." A working parent cannot complete a reporting requirement, misses a notice, works an irregular schedule, or cannot navigate a recertification system. The resulting loss of coverage is recorded as an "eligibility outcome" rather than a foreseeable product of bureaucratic design. This distinction matters because the government can produce enormous suffering without ever issuing a formal denial of human worth. It merely creates a procedural maze and declares that anyone who fails to navigate it has failed to qualify. The cruelty is placed one administrative step away from the decision-maker. The ACA itself has not literally been "revoked from tens of millions," and we should not use language opponents can easily disprove. The more accurate indictment is substantial enough: enhanced premium subsidies expired, the 2025 law restricted access to marketplace assistance, and its Medicaid provisions are expected to remove coverage from millions of people. CBO now projects that the uninsured population will rise from about 30 million in 2026 to 37 million by 2036, largely because of the reconciliation law's effects on Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace enrollment. That means millions more people living with the knowledge that any diagnosis could become a financial debt/death sentence. Healthcare debt is already widespread among the insured as well as the uninsured. KFF found that 41 percent of adults carried some form of debt caused by medical or dental bills. Among people with healthcare debt, roughly one-third reported damage to their credit, while others reported lawsuits, bankruptcy, foreclosure, or eviction. Another recent review found that almost one-third of working-age adults were carrying medical or dental debt and described medical debt as a leading contributor to bankruptcy. This is what privatized healthcare does to the kill line. It does not merely leave some people untreated. It turns sickness into a debt-generating event that can destabilize housing, employment, transportation, credit, and family life all at once. Even a person with insurance may face premiums, deductibles, copays, coinsurance, uncovered prescriptions, out-of-network charges, or a denied claim. They may be "covered" in every political talking point and still be financially unable to use the coverage. In America, healthcare is not simply a service. It is one of the mechanisms by which a person can be pushed from ordinary life into permanent precarity. Poverty Is Not Just Permitted. It Is Enforced. Perhaps the clearest evidence of how deliberately American policy prevents vulnerable people from developing resilience is the federal Supplemental Security Income asset limit. In 2026, an individual receiving SSI may have no more than $2,000 in countable resources. A couple may have no more than $3,000. Those limits have not been raised since 1989. If they had kept pace with inflation, they would now be approximately $5,275 for an individual and $7,913 for a couple --still hardly wealth, but at least enough to absorb some ordinary emergencies. In 1989, members of Congress earned $89,500 a year, while an individual receiving SSI was permitted only $2,000 in countable resources. Today, members of Congress receive $174,000--but the disabled person's limit is still $2,000. Congress nearly doubled its own salary while leaving disabled Americans trapped under a resource ceiling written for an economy that disappeared decades ago. Think about what $2,000 means in the present economy. It may not cover one month's rent in many American cities. It may not cover a car repair. It may not cover a medical deductible, emergency travel, a replacement appliance, a security deposit and first month's rent, or the cost of escaping an unsafe home. This is not a benefit system that tolerates poverty as an unfortunate condition. It is a system that requires poverty as a condition of continued assistance. The rule is sometimes summarized as "disabled people are not allowed to possess more than $2,000." Technically, there are exclusions: generally, the home in which a person lives, one vehicle used for transportation, certain burial funds, some trusts, and other defined categories are not counted. But the underlying accusation remains entirely valid. Cash, bank accounts, investments, some property, and other assets that could be used for food or shelter count against the limit. If an individual begins a month over the limit, they can lose SSI eligibility for that month. Even borrowed money left unspent into the following month can become a "countable resource." In other words, the system tells disabled people that they must remain nearly incapable of surviving an emergency in order to prove they need help. It prevents the accumulation of precisely the buffer that would keep a person above the kill line. And marriage doesn't improve the situation. Two eligible people do not receive two individual $2,000 limits. They receive a combined limit of $3,000. Their economic punishment is deepened by forming a household. And you wonder why fewer and fewer people are forming households? Congressional policy decisions have dictated these terms of survival. Ordinary people are just trying to live within then. Some Medicare Savings Programs now have higher asset limits, and Medicaid rules vary by state and program, so we should not collapse every senior, Medicare, Medicaid, or DSHS program into a single $1,500 or $2,000 rule. For example, federal Medicare Savings Program limits can be substantially higher, while Washington's aged, blind, and disabled Medicaid programs apply their own income and resource standards. But the larger architecture is unmistakable. Across many means-tested programs, poor, elderly, and disabled people must submit to intrusive financial tests and remain below strict resource ceilings to receive the support that keeps them alive. The rules differ, the exclusions differ, and the numbers differ, but the organizing principle is consistent: assistance is frequently conditioned not merely on having low income but on having no reserve. The government does not simply wait until vulnerable people fall below the kill line. It often makes remaining near that line a condition of aid. That is a moral obscenity hidden inside an eligibility formula. Then Make the Essentials More Expensive These benefit cuts and asset restrictions are landing at a time when the cost of basic life in increasingly punishing. In June 2026, consumer prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. Food prices were up 3%, shelter 3.3%, hospital services 5.1%, and vehicle maintenance and repair 7%. Over just one year - and costs have been rising consistently for many years. Gasoline prices, despite falling sharply in June from the previous month, remained 27% higher than one year earlier after the energy shock associated with the Iran war. Which, conveniently, has made billionaires and mega-corporations richer, while destroying the rest of us. Note that a single monthly decline does not erase the increase people already absorbed. When gasoline rises abruptly and then retreats partway, people do not receive refunds for the months in which they spent more getting to work, taking children to school, reaching medical appointments, or delivering goods. Higher fuel costs spread through transportation and supply chains, eventually appearing in the price of nearly everything else. Look at the inversion: The grocery bill rises while food assistance is cut. The cost of getting to work rises while access to healthcare remains tied to employment. The cost of housing rises while one missed payment can begin an eviction. The cost of repairing a vehicle rises in a country where reliable transportation is often a prerequisite for holding a job at all. Meanwhile, the labor market offers less reassurance than political slogans suggest. In June, the economy added only 57,000 nonfarm jobs, while unemployment stood at 4.2 percent - by the cooked numbers, not the real ones. Measured employment declined in leisure and hospitality, a sector on which many working-class families depend. The point is not that no one can find work. It is that "get a job" is not a serious social policy when available jobs may be unstable, inadequately paid, geographically inaccessible, incompatible with disability or caregiving, or insufficient to cover housing and healthcare. A job is only a route away from the kill line when it pays enough to create margin. Too many American jobs do not. This is how a country can post employment figures, celebrate economic growth, and still leave millions of people feeling, accurately, that there is nowhere to go. They are working. They are participating. They are producing. Yet the distance between their income and the cost of survival keeps narrowing. Their paychecks keep the extraction system operating. They do not necessarily keep the household safe. Once People Fall, Withdraw the Route Back The most chilling part of the kill-line analysis is not simply what happens before someone falls. It is what the system does after there is no more financial value to extract. America spends extraordinary amounts of money containing collapse while refusing to fund recovery at the same scale. We pay for emergency rooms after preventive care was inaccessible. We pay police to move homeless people from one block to another. We pay contractors to clear encampments. We pay jail costs for behavior rooted in untreated illness. We pay for temporary shelters while failing to build sufficient permanent supportive housing. We administer suffering through an archipelago of agencies, vendors, courts, hospitals, nonprofits, and law-enforcement systems. The money moves. The person does not necessarily recover. This is where this administration's new position on disability rights becomes profoundly important. In its June 18, 2026 opinion, the Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel argued that neither Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act nor Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act imposed an "integration mandate" requiring states to serve people with severe mental illness or disabilities in integrated community settings. It further argued that the Supreme Court's 1999 decision in Olmstead v. L.C. did not hold that those laws require states to provide treatment in the most integrated setting appropriate to a person's needs. That points to a return of the asylum. I'm sure America's for-profit incarceration companies CoreCivic and GEO Group will be thrilled. The memorandum does not itself repeal the ADA or overturn Olmstead. An executive-branch legal opinion cannot simply erase a Supreme Court decision. But the federal government is one of the most powerful enforcers of disability law. When the Justice Department announces that it rejects the legal foundation beneath decades of integration enforcement, it is telling states, institutions, courts, and families how this administration intends to use--or decline to use--that power. The practical question is not only whether a court will formally reverse Olmstead. It is whether states will feel freer to underfund home- and community-based services, expand institutional placements, resist integration agreements, or defend unnecessary confinement while the federal government retreats from enforcement. Let's look at what "institutionalization" has meant in American history: elderly people, disabled people, mentally ill people, children, inconvenient women, and others stripped of autonomy and warehoused behind doors they did not control. Stripped of dignity, agency, and rights, with zero due process. At Danvers State Hospital, patients could see the surrounding world through the institution's many windows while being denied the ability to reenter it. Hundreds were buried under numbered markers rather than names. History matters - and is worth deeper reading - because institutionalization has never been applied only to a neat, medically objective category of people. The dominant class always imagines "disability" as something that happens to someone else. But disability is not a fixed caste. It is an accident, an illness, a stroke, dementia, long COVID, a workplace injury, a difficult birth, a degenerative disease, a war wound, or simply the eventual vulnerability of an aging body. You may be autonomous until the morning you cannot climb your stairs. You may be respected until the day you need help bathing. You may be treated as competent until a relative, physician, court, insurer, or state agency decides otherwise. And historically, the category of the "unfit" has expanded whenever powerful people found expansion convenient. Women were institutionalized for disobedience. Queer people were classified as diseased. Black, Indigenous, immigrant, and poor families were subjected to eugenic policy, coerced sterilization, medical abuse, family separation, and confinement. Poverty itself has repeatedly been treated as evidence of moral or mental deficiency. That is why weakening community-integration rights is not a narrow technical adjustment affecting a small population elsewhere. It alters the balance of power between vulnerable human beings and the institutions authorized to have power over their lives. Is This a Policy of Getting Rid of "Undesirables"? We should ask the question plainly because euphemism has become one of the principal tools by which "democracies" conceal cruelty. Does this amount to a coordinated, procedural,deniableeffort to rid the country of people considered undesirable? I do not have evidence of a central directive ordering government agencies to eliminate disabled, poor, elderly, sick, or unhoused Americans. I would not make that factual claim without such evidence. But intent is not the only morally relevant category in public policy. There is also knowledge. There is foreseeability. There is repeated choice.There is the decision to proceed after the consequences have been documented. The government knows that people lose healthcare when eligibility is narrowed and administrative burdens are increased. It knows that people go hungry when SNAP is cut. It knows that a $2,000 asset limit prevents disabled people from building an emergency reserve. It knows that rising housing, food, energy, and medical costs place households under intensifying pressure. It knows that community-based care allows elderly and disabled people to remain with families, preserve autonomy, and avoid unnecessary institutional confinement. It knows that people who lose housing are exposed to violence, illness, exploitation, sleep deprivation, criminalization, and premature death. These are not obscure consequences. They are the subjects of budget scores, administrative records, litigation, academic studies, inspector-general reports, public testimony, and decades of lived experience. When leaders know these outcomes and continue removing the protections anyway, "unintended consequences" becomes an insult to logic and language. The defensible conclusion is not that every official involved shares a private desire to kill vulnerable people. Systems do not require unanimity of motive. One official may be pursuing tax cuts. Another may be protecting an industry. Another may believe suffering creates work incentives. Another may be hostile to disability rights. Another may be indifferent. Another may simply be advancing a career by implementing the order in front of them. Fragmented motives can still produce a coherent machine. The machine being assembled now does several things at once. It transfers wealth upward. It makes access to necessities more difficult, expensive, and conditional. It requires vulnerable people to remain asset-poor. It increases the number of uninsured, food-insecure, and homeless people. It weakens federal enforcement of the right to receive care outside institutions. It treats hardship as an individual defect. And it preserves punitive, for-profit systems to contain people once they have fallen. Whether or not its architects publicly use the word "undesirable," the policy increasingly distinguishes between people whose health, labor, wealth, or obedience makes them valuable to the dominant order and people treated primarily as costs. The latter are not necessarily killed directly. They are made more killable. They are denied the resources that prevent premature death. They are exposed to conditions known to shorten life. They are placed in systems where neglect is dispersed among enough actors that no single person has to feel responsible. Their disappearance occurs gradually: from the workforce, from housing, from community life, from public view, and finally from life itself. That is how a procedural state commits moral violence while preserving plausible deniability. No one signs the death certificate with the cause of death: "policy." A Government Can Kill by Abandonment We have been trained to recognize state violence primarily when it takes the form of a weapon, a prison cell, a deportation van, or a uniformed officer. Those forms are real, terribly real, and the administration's campaign of raids, detention, xenophobia, racial targeting, and expulsion deserves its own full accounting. But governments also harm through subtraction. They withdraw medication. Food. Income. The doctor. The home-care worker. The case manager. The legal protection that kept a person in their community. They withdraw the public institution that once answered the phone, processed the claim, investigated the abuse, or enforced the right. Then they point to the ruined person and call the ruin evidence of personal failure. This is why the "kill line" is more than a viral phrase. It reveals the connective tissue among policies usually discussed separately. SNAP cuts are not merely agricultural policy. Medicaid cuts are not merely health policy. The SSI asset ceiling is not merely an outdated technical limit. Housing scarcity is not merely a local zoning problem. Weakening Olmstead enforcement is not merely a disagreement among lawyers. Together, they determine whether a human being has enough margin to survive a shock, whether they can accumulate the resources to recover, whether they remain connected to a community, and whether the state recognizes an obligation to help them return. That is the line between a society and a sorting mechanism. A functioning civilization does not guarantee that no one will ever fall. Illness, grief, disability, addiction, economic disruption, and bad decisions will always exist. Its moral test is whether falling behind becomes a permanent sentence. Can a person get sick without losing their home? Can a disabled person save enough to survive a broken transmission in their car? Can a mother leave an abusive household without becoming homeless? Can a worker lose a job without losing healthcare? Can an elderly person receive care in the home they have lived in for fifty years? Can a person experience addiction or mental illness and still be treated as someone whose life has a future? Can someone make a mistake and remain a member of society? The answer being constructed by this government is increasingly: only if the market still finds you useful, your family can privately absorb the cost, or you possess enough wealth to purchase your own mercy. For everyone else, the margin is being narrowed. The floor is being lowered. The ladder back up is being pulled away. We do not need to invent a conspiracy to see what is happening. We need only follow the appropriations, eligibility rules, legal opinions, price data, coverage losses, and human consequences to their shared destination. America's kill line is not merely an economic condition anymore. It is becoming an instrument of governance. And the first obligation of anyone seeking power in this moment is to say so--before millions more people are pushed across it and blamed for the fall. Care. Courage. Peter,

The ink was barely dry on last night's primary results when the attacks started.

Cook Political Report downgraded our Senate race from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." That is not a clerical change. **[That is the left wing media signaling to every left-wing donor in America that they believe that Texas is in play.](https://links.iterable.com/s/c/80koxcbs8HmZKnLEjjHrGSS9N5eyKdQemxz-afKeeIrv4fVOaIwvFbdEq59q49JmqLRN4xCJMABfG7t0czTl6OT6OIDssl5kKAgutMIRhbu37J2fAFb6mXMZxDKM6gcI-8lk8CgKahZNGlTewaVUqjFQKogGlVGGaPZaqHsnIrJcXBdLSjRQw-SHBD_aI5FbffEDox8NpavefzApEXCpSJbZ6yV8xZxKmFgnTaV93excyURhfuvsWyvKJgwjzqR9j1UOLpY2_1bN6RQf68690600MpdOtBYy3m-uB-q7ivpKhI4ZAkKW8EhA1glF1T6TFeDdyrqWl_WUWlAZN3jweWLYZ2-p1BXnC4XqHDV1TMOSSy1R8E2dCPkBsVqk3Xs6fsVBeeBZLwQ8cXSs-EllBK5oCbgF9ZhsmgimPsmZ-ePEbM5KJnukd6m05eON_CzxKRbrQQxPjzw6Mb2-9QqZu6YqiG4a_nEz8Wl-5cI4YnlcvPILDnpv-A-TqBubdvilBBj8EMTdOMw_zNyL0S-xm3SmucXm0UFzF2R5EqsBJm3ruD-hNf7Edv4mdtCwLHF0xgqrlIN04JZyRFve22QJABkJNMtjyHCYeQ4qtQNIA8W6z33-9-syLvm7FNOX5htInjDiYklAgJJeFWkNeIBEkaRRU0AMShxBMafX9hWJ62j5_cWgibOMOx96BxSjHLFb3LpTXTK1NMEgZr6Wmpt7Vq-CAh9_kOFoQlCIb_2h46d8l5taNblijDt6w7KZ0Lf5SPP1fXNdNX5Hxv1_jJg9E_xtWGWKGVyYPResGEt4vTTSvnAV324zn06g_gokLzXHOv_F5R9Mx6FOOVTVdeacVj_bj0NKPK_g9zQJiXFuM7Jhi3dHUCny26mOXpacKXuoFujNLYJk84xV9OTQ-uaYGSXycJRfhoHwYS_WXlJcoq_5ccqfuX55vf-55vHm0yEWWmnGLFKyGfNXmB2y4XSgFCtqicXjd3LoFbkIHc7llAYZAxkUIJqrvVG3dXsroSG79Gf4uFIbweK-5DI63a3RPLshfBwDx7Eoy2IyefU/HEQ8Cy0DefeWHya9hX7M3BZbpX_Tf3Ll/23)**

The Democrats and their allies in the media have been waiting for this moment. Now they have it. And within hours of our runoff victory, they are already targeting us.

Here is what Cook Political Report's Jessica Taylor wrote this morning: _Talarico has a "fundraising edge" that Paxton must overcome._

The Democrats and their allies in the media are doing everything in their power to expand that edge in order to flip a Senate seat.

subject: How prediction markets are corrupting the news
body:
[ https://act.couriernewsroom.com/go/398?t=1005&refcode=20260727_Prediction&akid=174%2E344797%2EXAm-Vx ]COURIER Newsroom

Hi Peter,

For two years, the story of the American news media has been fear of
Donald Trump and a willingness to put profits ahead of what's best for our
democracy.

Now there's a quieter threat. It's the same one [ https://act.couriernewsroom.com/go/575?t=1003&refcode=20260727_Prediction&akid=174%2E344797%2EXAm-Vx ]COURIER's Mark Jacob
wrote about earlier this week: prediction markets like Kalshi.

Before we continue, COURIER is one of the fastest growing independent
local news outlets in the country. [ https://act.couriernewsroom.com/go/398?t=1007&refcode=20260727_Prediction&akid=174%2E344797%2EXAm-Vx ]We rely on grassroots
support, and we'd be grateful for your donation of any amount
today.

[ https://act.couriernewsroom.com/go/398?t=1008&refcode=20260727_Prediction&akid=174%2E344797%2EXAm-Vx ]Chip in

Popular Information's Judd Legum and Public Notice's Aaron Rupar conducted
incredible reporting documenting what happened after CNN and CNBC signed
deals with Kalshi, one of the largest prediction markets. These platforms
let people bet on politics and world events, and the insider trading
problem is no longer hypothetical: Trump's longtime teleprompter operator
is in settlement talks with federal regulators over roughly $90,000 he
allegedly made betting on what the president would say in his own
speeches.

Here's what they found (you can [ https://act.couriernewsroom.com/go/576?t=1004&refcode=20260727_Prediction&akid=174%2E344797%2EXAm-Vx ]see and support their work here):

* CNN has run at least 115 segments built on Kalshi's data.
* Since April, CNBC has had a dedicated reporter producing articles that
amount to writing up Kalshi markets as news.
* CNBC's own disclosure describes a commercial relationship with Kalshi
that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment. In at
least 22 cases, that disclosure was missing entirely.

CNBC says it discloses commercial relationships when they're directly
relevant to the story.

This corruption from the news media is quieter than a threatening Truth
Social post. No subpoena. No FCC letter. Just a network deciding that a
company it profits from counts as a news source, and telling viewers about
the arrangement only sometimes.

Fear you can see. This you can't.

body:
Don’t let Washington elites call the shots

| [](https://trk.emails.susancollinsformaine._ZXhpdGludGVudD10cnVlP3JlY3VycmluZz10cnVlJmFtb3VudD00NSZleF90aWQ9MjAyNjA3MjdfRlEtVEsuMTEwMTE3X3QxOTY5ODY3LTExNDImdXRtX2NhbXBhaWduPTIwMjYwNzI3X0ZRLVRLLjExMDExN190MTk2OTg2Ny0xMTQyIn0/P6ZUX9epVYlmAtzn-QRr9A)

The word is out. Chuck Schumer and Maine Democrats have decided Troy Jackson is their guy.They’ve huddled in backrooms, looked at their map, and hand-picked exactly who they want representing Maine in the U.S. Senate.But they forgot one major detail: Maine’s Senate seat belongs to the people of Maine.Chuck Schumer wants a rubber stamp in Washington. | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. clean_body: Harlan Crow gave the maximum allowable contribution to his campaign. | | | Pennsylvanians should be furious, Peter. Harlan Crow, one of the Republican Party's most notorious billionaire megadonors, just gave the maximum contribution federal law allows to Sen. John Fetterman's campaign. Crow isn't just any megadonor. He's spent decades using his fortune to bankroll Republican politicians, fund the far-right agenda, and buy influence at the highest levels of government. For more than 20 years, he secretly showered Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas with luxury vacations, private jet travel, real estate deals, and private school tuition for Thomas's family — all while Thomas ruled on cases affecting the interests of the country's wealthiest people. Now, Harlan Crow is writing checks to John Fetterman.And if billionaire megadonors are going all-in to keep Fetterman in the Senate, then it's up to us to build the grassroots campaign that can defeat him. **** According to new reporting from The Intercept, Crow contributed $7,000 to Fetterman’s campaign on June 30th. Less than a week later, Fetterman formed a joint fundraising committee with Republican Sen. Dave McCormick.1 This didn’t happen in a vacuum. Since taking office, Fetterman has broken with Democrats to side with Republicans and the Trump administration on immigration, presidential nominees, military action abroad, and other major issues. Now, the same Republican billionaire donor class that's spent decades buying influence and dragging our country to the right is investing in him, too. Pennsylvanians didn't elect John Fetterman to represent billionaires like Harlan Crow. We elected him to fight for working people, stand up to billionaire power, and answer to the communities that sent him to Washington. And if Fetterman won’t be that senator, then working people deserve a real choice. That’s why we're doing the work now to find, recruit, and support a genuine working-class champion who can take him on in the Democratic primary. Taking on an incumbent senator backed by billionaires won’t be easy. We’ll never match donors like Harlan Crow dollar for dollar. But we don't have to, Peter. If thousands of people across Pennsylvania organize, volunteer, and chip in what they can, we can build the grassroots campaign it takes to win. subject: I’ve been doing this a long time
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Pappas for Senate
body:
I feel a personal connection to Chris.
[](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260727_1.n3qune&refcode=em20260727-1&t=1&akid=7965%2E582294%2ESpOz4Q)
Friends,
I’ve spent a long time watching and participating in politics in New England, and one thing I know for sure is that the toughest races are often the most important ones.
**That’s exactly the kind of race Chris Pappas is running in New Hampshire.**
Chris represents one of the most competitive districts in the country – he’s won it four times by doing what strong leaders do: showing up, listening to voters, and focusing on the issues that matter most to working families.
**[But, New Hampshire is not a guaranteed blue state. Chris needs support from all of us if we want to defend this Senate seat for Democrats and push towards retaking the Majority in Washington. Will you step up and chip in $5 to fuel his campaign?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260727_1.n3qune&refcode=em20260727-1&t=2&akid=7965%2E582294%2ESpOz4Q)**
I also feel a personal connection to Chris. Like me, he’s a proud Greek American who grew up in a family that believed in hard work and public service. Those values are deeply reflected in how Chris approaches his work in Congress.
But anyone who follows politics knows that seats like this are always a top target for Republicans.
_That’s why early grassroots support matters so much._
**[Chris has proven he knows how to win tough races in New Hampshire. With your support, he’ll have the resources he needs to do it again.
