There's a federal comment window on 887 acres in Chesterfield that closes tomorrow (July 28th).
_You 're receiving this because you signed up for updates from Jason Knapp's campaign for Congress in VA-01. This is our home for longer writing. Unsubscribe anytime below._
Thanks for reading Jason Knapp! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
[Pledge your support](https://substack..ExSxk4UJF3umbWCLL5BpNs77l1ucm5h8RgpiFscDC64?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=208709778)
**The short version**
The Army Corps of Engineers is taking public comments on Google's [Project Skye](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/57d59ab6-2c70-4332-9390-45e006e833c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), an 887-acre data center campus in Chesterfield County. The permit would fill in, permanently erasing, about 18 acres of forested wetland and a mile and a half of stream. **Comments close TOMORROW, Tuesday, July 28.** Docket NAO-2026-00282.
**Why write.** This is the only point in the entire approval where somebody is legally required to take what you say, put it in a permanent public record, and answer it. The rezoning happened four years ago. The land was sold last summer. Six hundred people asked questions at Google's open houses recently and not one word of it was written down anywhere as part of any official record. This is different, and nothing here has been decided yet.
**Ask for a public hearing.** Any person can, in writing, during the comment period. The Corps has to grant it unless it finds the issues raised are insubstantial. That's a low bar, and whether it gets cleared comes down to how many people raise something real.
**Four things worth raising:**
1. **The impacts table isn 't in the public file.** There are drawings and information contained within ten sheets. Nine were published. Every one of those nine drawings points to a table on the tenth. Strangely, nobody outside the applicant can check a single number in this permit.
2. **The state paused its review on July 23, 2026** because the application wasn't complete. The public's deadline is five days after that.
3. **Almost all of the stream being filled is headwater channel.** The wide corridors at the edges of the property are left alone. What gets filled are the small draws at the top of the system, and those are the ones doing the flood storage and filtration work.
4. **The rest of the buildout isn 't counted.** A road corridor, transmission work, and another campus are drawn on Google's own exhibits and left out of this permit's math.

**How to comment, three ways:**
• Our step-by-step walkthrough: **[jasonknappforcongress.com/comment](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/0c72d76e-8332-4af9-939a-b4e672aaa241?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
• Direct to the Corps: **[rrs.usace.army.mil/rrs](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/ef31729a-6058-417b-8097-674dc0b9ef98?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
• By email: **CENAO.REG_ROD@usace.army.mil** (put NAO-2026-00282 in the subject line)
The public notice and drawings are **[here](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/57d59ab6-2c70-4332-9390-45e006e833c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**.
It takes about five minutes. You don't have to live in Chesterfield, you don't have to live in Virginia, and you don't have to be an expert. You need to be a concerned citizen in this country. If you are reading this, that is likely, you.
**A note before you start.**
This runs long. The important part is above, and I hope you'll file.
The rest is here because the process is the story. What's happening on Deep Creek is running in other counties right now, same steps, same order. Knowing the outcome won't help you with the next one. Knowing how the decision gets made lets you explain it to a neighbor over a fence, and tells you which things are worth saying to a federal agency.
If five minutes is all you've got, the box above is the whole ask.
I put water ahead of the power side of this on purpose. (That piece, who pays to build the grid and why your bill keeps climbing, goes out later.) Power problems are expensive, and expensive problems can be fixed. You can build generation. You can rewrite a rate structure. You can move a cost from one column to another. But a wetland that gets filled in does not come back, and an aquifer that takes on salt water does not come back. Not in our lifetimes, and not in our grandchildren's. Money is recoverable. Water, in the two forms I'm about to describe, is not.
**I learned how to think about water at sea, where the accounting is straightforward.**
On a ship, you make your own water. Evaporators run around the clock turning seawater into fresh, and every gallon in the tank is accounted for. When the evaporators go down, you go to what we call "water hours".
Here's the thing about water hours. The engineer knows the exact number of gallons left. The kid on the third deck doesn't know the number, and doesn't need to. He knows his shower just went from five minutes to one, and he knows exactly why. Nobody has to explain it to him. Nobody pretends it isn't happening.
Virginia is approving some of the largest industrial water users in the Commonwealth's history right now. Most people have no idea it's happening, and almost nobody can tell you the number. That's the part I want to fix. But before we can, we have to be clear about what's actually being argued over, because it isn't one thing.
**THREE PROBLEMS, NOT ONE**
I hear this at candidate forums, at meet-and-greets, at supervisor meetings, sitting with watermen down on the water and with farmers whose families have worked the same ground for generations. Everybody says "the water issue" like it's one thing.
It isn't. Data centers put pressure on Virginia's water in three different ways, and where you live determines which one is coming for you.
**In Northern Virginia, the problem is how much they take out.** Loudoun County draws its water from the Potomac River and Goose Creek, and that supply is backstopped by reservoirs upstream in Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia. The county also built about twenty miles of pipeline to send treated wastewater to data centers for cooling instead of drinking water (roughly 736 million gallons of it in 2024). Even with all that, Northern Virginia's data centers used close to two billion gallons in 2023, up 63 percent from 2019. That's a real strain on a river. But a river refills. Next spring's rain puts it back.
**In the Richmond corridor, the problem is what gets destroyed.** This one isn't about pumping at all. It's about filling in the wetlands and streams that hold, cool, and clean the water in the first place, and putting a building on top of them. Once that's done, it doesn't matter how efficient the cooling system is. What was lost is lost.
**On the Northern Neck and the Middle Peninsula, the problem is that we can 't get it back.** No big river intake. No reservoir agreement. What we have is deep groundwater that is already declining and already at risk of turning salty.
Three different mechanisms. One industry. And because each county only ever sees its own version of it, every county fights this alone, and none of them can see that they're all up against the same playbook.
That is the whole argument for a federal floor, and I'll come back to it.
**WHAT 'S HAPPENING RIGHT NOW: 887 ACRES ON DEEP CREEK**
Google has three data center campuses planned in Chesterfield County. The largest is called Project Skye. It's 887.7 acres in the Upper Magnolia Green area: five data center buildings and three substations, south of Genito Road and east of Moseley Road.**1**
The federal permit application is a public document, and you can read the whole thing yourself at the link above.
**Start with the names** , because the one on the permit and the one on the ground aren't quite the same. Google's own project site says the property is bounded to the south by the corridor of Horsepen Creek.**2** Otterdale Branch runs along the north. Those two feed Deep Creek, which runs to the Appomattox and then the James. Chesterfield opened a $100 million middle school named after Deep Creek last July, a mile and a half from here. The permit would permanently fill 17.99 acres of forested wetlands and 8,115 feet of stream channel. A mile and a half of creek. It would also convert another 7.23 acres of forested wetland into emergent wetland, which means the trees come out and what's left behind is marsh.**3**
Surveys of the property found 147 acres of wetlands and about six miles of streams on it altogether.**4** The proposal fills about 18 of those 147 acres and a mile and a half of those six miles. Twelve percent of the wetland. A quarter of the stream. Put that way it sounds like most of it survives.
**Which part survives matters more than how much.**
Picture the creek network on that property as a tree lying on its side. The main channel is the trunk. Branching off it are smaller and smaller draws, and out at the ends are the shallow ones that only run water after a rain.
The plan keeps the trunk. Those wide corridors along the south and east edges of the property aren't touched. Two of the ten drawing sheets cover that ground and have almost nothing marked on them.**5**
What gets filled are the branches and the twigs. Small draws threading up between the buildings and the equipment yards. Nearly every foot of the smallest channels on the property is in the fill.
That's backwards from how the system works. Water doesn't start in the main channel. It comes off the land into the small stuff first, and that's where most of the slowing and the filtering happens. Fill in the twigs and the trunk is still there, same name on the map. It's just getting raw, fast, unfiltered water now instead of what those small channels used to hand it.
**Who decides which streams count.**
There's a line in this process between a stream that gets a protective buffer and one that doesn't, and it comes down to how often water runs in it. Perennial channels, a channel that carries flowing water year round in a normal year, sustained between rain events by groundwater discharge, get a buffer under Virginia's Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act. The smaller ones mostly don't.
So somebody has to label them. Every channel on that property gets called perennial, intermittent, or ephemeral, and the label is what determines whether it's protected[[1]](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/1142a477-d155-4ecd-9781-3959de7811fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). The labeling was done by the applicant's consultant, who walked each channel and scored it.
On May 8, 2026 the state issued its determination letter for this property. It confirms where the water is. It does not confirm the labels. The letter says it outright: the approval doesn't include stream type.
So to me it would appear that the labels came from the applicant, the labels set the buffer line, and as far as we can tell, no agency has checked the labels.
To be clear, we are not saying that anyone or any agency "cooked the numbers". The scoring followed the standard method and the scores weren't close to the line. The Corps sent a biologist to walk the property in April, and she caught a mapping error the consultant had to fix. That's the system working.
She had the field data and the full drawing set. You and I have nine sheets of a set of ten.
The impact drawings run ten sheets. Nine were published. All nine points to an impacts table on the tenth, and the tenth isn't there, available for public review. That table is the only document that says which channel, how many feet, and where.
The notice says 8,115 feet of stream get filled. The February application, the newest file the public can reach, says 7,964. The 150-foot gap isn't the point. The point is that a total is all anyone outside the applicant can see, and totals move for reasons you can't audit when you cannot fully see how that total was calculated. After the April walk, one channel was reclassified, one shrank, and one came off the map entirely. A channel that carried a fill number in February is gone from the next inventory.
So ask for the tenth sheet. Not because 150 feet decides anything, but because you're being asked to weigh in on the size of this by Tuesday, using the only file you're allowed to open, and it isn't the one the agency is using.
**Why a wetland matters, in broad and plain terms.** A forested wetland isn't scenery. It's working infrastructure that the public never had to pay for. It soaks up stormwater during heavy rains and lets it out slowly over the following days, which is what keeps the creek from tearing out its own banks and keeps the road downstream from going under. It filters sediment and nitrogen out of the runoff before that water reaches the James River and, eventually, the Chesapeake Bay. And a wooded wetland does that job considerably better than a grassy one, because the trees, the deep root systems, and a century of leaf litter in the soil are doing most of the work. That's why converting seven acres from forest to marsh is a real loss even though a map would still label it "wetland."
**What mitigation credits do, and what they don 't.** To compensate for the loss, Google proposes to buy 43.31 wetland credits and 9,213 stream credits from approved mitigation banks.**9** A mitigation bank is a large wetland that somebody has restored or permanently protected in another location, and credits from it are sold to developers who are filling wetlands elsewhere.
Prior to mitigation banks, a developer filling wetlands would promise to build a small replacement nearby, and an enormous number of those failed. Five acres here, three acres there, nobody funding the upkeep, nobody checking back in ten years. Banking pools those obligations into large restoration sites that are professionally managed, legally protected in perpetuity, and finished before the damage is done rather than promised afterward. Measured across an entire watershed or an entire state, that usually produces a better result for the environment than what came before it. It certainly isn't perfect, and there are shortcomings, but it is largely a step forward from past practices.
The limitation is the one that matters if you live here. The benefit a wetland provides is local. The flood storage protects the road just below it, not a road forty miles away. The filtering cleans the water in that particular creek. So, when the replacement acres are established in a different watershed (for the neighboring Project Loch campus, the proposed preservation sits in the South Anna River watershed, on the far side of Richmond), the ledger balances, but the geography doesn't. The Chesapeake Bay may come out closer to even. Deep Creek does not.
In my view, this means that the trade gets made at one level but the consequences land at another. A company, a mitigation bank, and a federal agency settle it in acres and credits. The family whose road goes under when Deep Creek can no longer hold heavy rains was never a party to that transaction. They had no seat at it and no vote in it, and they pay for it in the only currency they've got, which is their own daily life. Nobody who lives on Deep Creek gets a wetland back.
Now look at the legend on those drawings. It includes layers for a road permitted by others, for future Dominion development, and for a transmission easement. Google's own site plan, dated this month, labels that road corridor the future Powhite Parkway extension, alongside a Mount Hermon Road extension, a Westerleigh Parkway extension, and the location of another technology campus.**10** Their site also says they'll design and pay for a public sewer main running along Horsepen Creek, the one corridor this permit leaves alone.
All of that is drawn on the applicant's own exhibits. None of it is counted in this permit's impact math. Each piece gets reviewed by itself, if it gets reviewed at all, and the total never appears in one place.
The historic properties review in that federal file is still open, and the notice specifically invites public comment on it. On species, the Corps finished its consultation on listed bat species in June. The monarch butterfly is proposed for listing and isn't covered by the determination the Corps used.**11**
The timing matters too. On June 26, three days before the Corps opened this comment period, Virginia DEQ sent the applicant another round of questions on the same submittal. The applicant answered July 10. On July 23, DEQ said that answer wasn't complete and paused its review.**12** The state's file is still being assembled, and the federal comment window closes first.
None of this is decided. That's the whole point of what comes next.
**HOW THAT LAND GOT TO THIS POINT**
This is the part I'd ask you to sit with, **because it 's a pattern and not an accident.**
The Skye property was rezoned in May 2022, when the Chesterfield Board of Supervisors approved 1,728 acres at Upper Magnolia Green for a technology park. That vote was 3 to 2. Two supervisors asked to hold it over for more work, lost that motion, and then voted no.
It was rezoned again in May 2025, when the county's Economic Development Authority moved about 980 more acres, with roughly 870 of those restricted to data center use. At the time, the filing referred only to a confidential economic development project. Google was not named publicly.
The land sold in July 2025 for nearly $60 million.
And the federal wetlands review, the first time anyone publicly counted the 147 acres of wetlands and six miles of stream on that ground, is happening now, in 2026.
Read those four dates in order. Zoned. Zoned again. Sold. Surveyed.
The survey came last. So, when the supervisors voted, and when the land changed hands for nearly $60 million, there was no public document saying how much wetland or how much stream was on that property. Nobody in that room had the number, because the number didn't exist yet.
The public got two turns to speak, and both of them landed off by a step. At the rezoning, residents could argue about whether data centers belonged out there. What nobody could tell them was what it would cost the creeks, because nobody had counted the creeks yet. Now they can comment on the creeks. The zoning is finished and the land has changed hands.
Both times, the information you'd need to answer the question was on the other side of the decision.
Nobody broke a rule here, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Every step in that sequence was legal, and most of it happened in open meetings. That's exactly why it's worth talking about. The sequence itself is the problem, and the same sequence is running in county after county.
Chesterfield has since changed its ordinance. Data centers there can no longer be built by right; a new one now requires a conditional use permit and a public hearing. That's a genuine improvement and the county and its Supervisors deserve credit for it.
All three Google sites had already been approved under the old rules.
That's why rezoning applications across this district are moving at the speed they are. Forty-six data center bills were carried over from this year's General Assembly session into 2027. Everyone in this business can read a legislative calendar. Get the land entitled now, and whatever Richmond writes next year applies to the next company, not to the parcel you have already locked down.
Speed is a strategy. And look at who it's being run against.
A county board of supervisors is five people. In most of our counties it's a part-time job with a small stipend. The people holding those seats are farmers, small business owners, retired teachers, a nurse, somebody who runs a marina. They meet at night, after their regular work. They have a county attorney, and a planning staff you could fit in a pickup truck.
On the other side of the table is a team of land use attorneys, hydrologists, transmission engineers, and site selection consultants who have run this exact process in a hundred counties and will run it in a hundred more.
We are asking those five neighbors of ours to become working experts in wetland delineation and aquifer science, at a night meeting, in three-minute increments, while they're also trying to close a budget gap and maybe trying to figure out how to afford to replace a high school roof.
That is not a fair fight. And when it goes badly, it is not their failure. It's the failure of every level of government above them that refused to set a standard they could stand on.
**WHAT 'S COMING FOR US: THE MISTAKE YOU CAN'T UNDO**
Now the Northern Neck. I'll say plainly that this part is personal for me. Our family home is in Reedville, and the water I'm about to describe is the water under my own house and my neighbors' houses.
Most of eastern Virginia (the Northern Neck, the Middle Peninsula, everything east of I-95) sits inside what the state calls the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area. There is no big river intake out here and no reservoir agreement. What we have is deep groundwater: the Potomac Aquifer, which supplies about 70 percent of everything withdrawn in that management area, and the Piney Point aquifer, which the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula draw from directly.
It is already in trouble. Water levels in parts of the system have dropped by as much as 200 feet. A study by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ, the state agency that regulates water withdrawals) found that average levels in the Potomac Aquifer have been falling since 2021. The state is now steering localities away from it; Caroline County is being pushed toward taking water from the Rappahannock River instead.
Hold these two facts side by side. The Commonwealth is telling counties out here to get off the aquifer. And this industry is moving south down I-95 and east along I-64, looking for the next county willing to zone for it.
Our version is worse, and this is the mechanism. When you pump hard on a coastal aquifer, you don't just lower the water level. You change the direction the water moves underground. Groundwater here used to flow generally east, toward the coast. Decades of heavy pumping have reversed that, pulling water inland toward the wells and downward into the deepest layers. The boundary between fresh water and saltwater moves right along with it. The places most at risk are the ones closest to salt water, and the Northern Neck is a peninsula with the Chesapeake Bay on one side, the Potomac on the other, and the Rappahannock underneath.
There's a second effect on top of that one. As an aquifer loses pressure, the ground above it compacts and settles. The Virginia coastal plain is sinking about one to three millimeters a year and combined with rising seas that produces five to eight millimeters of change annually in some places. Deeper wells, higher water, more flooding. All from the same cause.
An over-drawn river refills. An aquifer that goes salty does not. Not in your lifetime and not in your grandchildren's. Northern Virginia's water mistakes are expensive. Ours would be permanent.
And this ought to bother everybody out here. Inside a groundwater management area, you need a state permit to withdraw 300,000 gallons or more in a month.**13** Household wells fall well below that and aren't reported at all. So, the families with the most to lose, everyone on a private well from Reedville to Deltaville to Lanexa, don't appear anywhere in the state's data. If your well turns brackish, there is no state record that it ever existed.
**ONE ROOM WHERE YOU COUNT, AND ONE WHERE YOU DON 'T**
Here is the gap that made me want to write this.
When a project fills in wetlands or streams, it needs a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. And that permit comes with something almost nothing else has in this whole process: a legal obligation to hear from you.
The Corps publishes public notices and opens a comment period. Every comment becomes part of the official record, and that record is public. The Corps uses those comments to evaluate the project's impacts, to prepare its environmental review, and to weigh what the regulation calls the public interest. That list specifically includes water quality, water supply and conservation, flood hazards, and, in the actual words of the rule, the needs and welfare of the people.**14** The evaluation is required to account for cumulative impacts, not this one project in isolation.
And here's the part most people have never been told. Any person can request a public hearing in writing during the comment period. In the Corps' own language in this very notice: requests for a public hearing will be granted, unless the District Engineer determines that the issues raised are insubstantial or there is otherwise no valid interest to be served by a hearing.**15**
Not "may consider." Granted. And if they say no, they have to say why.
Be precise about what's up for decision here, because it changes what's worth writing. The comment period isn't in question. It's running right now and it closes on Tuesday, July 28th. What hasn't been decided is the hearing.
The test isn't whether your comment is persuasive or well written. Read the standard again. The hearing happens unless the issues raised are insubstantial. That is a low bar, and it is the only bar, and it turns entirely on what people put in the file.
Set that against everything else in this process. A company can hold an open house where not one word said by a resident is written down anywhere. A county can adopt an overlay district that replaces public hearings with staff-level permits. A utility rate case can move through a commission most people have never heard of. But if a project fills waters of the United States, a federal agency has to put your objection in the file and answer for it.
Some people will call that a technicality. I call it one of the last pieces of working democratic machinery left in this process, and it does not belong to environmental lawyers or to anybody's side. It belongs to whoever shows up. That is true here, it is true across Virginia, and it is true in every county in this country where people are about to have a decision handed to them that they never got a vote on.
Now the room where you don't count.
Section 404 covers filling in water. It does not cover pumping water out.
That one distinction changes what your objection is worth. If a company wants to bulldoze a stream, a federal agency must publish a notice, take your comment, and grant you a hearing unless it finds your concerns insubstantial. If that same company wants to pump a million gallons a day out of the aquifer under your house, there's no federal notice at all. It's a state permit. Virginia does publish notice and take comment on those, and I want to be fair about that. But the hearing standard is different. At the state level a hearing may be held if the response is significant and there are substantial disputed issues.**16** Federally it must be held unless someone finds the opposite.
One is a presumption in your favor. The other is somebody's discretion. And for the water that matters most out here, we get the second one.
That gap didn't get there by accident, and Congress is the only place it can be closed.
A caveat, because I don't want to oversell what you've got here.
Project Skye gets an individual permit and a public notice because it's enormous. Most projects don't. The Clean Water Act also lets the Corps write general permits, which pre-authorize whole categories of work that the agency has determined will have no more than minimal effects. If your project fits inside a category, you don't get a public notice. You file a short notification, or sometimes nothing at all, and you go.
That's not a small side door. The nationwide permit program authorizes roughly 25,000 reported activities a year, plus about 30,000 more that don't require reporting at all.**17** Against that, the individual permits that generate a notice like this one are a rounding error.
Now the part that should stop you. The Corps reissued the nationwide permits this past January, effective in March and running through 2031.**18** In that reissuance, the permit covering commercial development was modified to name data centers explicitly, including, in the Corps' own words, artificial intelligence and machine learning facilities.**19** The category now has this industry's name written into it.
The limits are real. Half an acre of wetland loss, 300 feet of streambed. Skye is thirty-six times over that, which is exactly why we're getting a comment period. But look at how the streambed limit works: a district engineer can waive the 300 feet for intermittent and ephemeral channels by writing a determination that the effects are minimal.**20**
There it is again. The same line between a stream that counts and one that mostly doesn't, doing the same work, in a different rule.
Virginia adds a layer. The nationwide permit for commercial development is suspended here, replaced by a state programmatic general permit that the Corps and DEQ run together. The current one expires August 1st and a new five-year version takes its place the same day.**21** The public comment period on that reissuance ran last fall and closed in October. Almost nobody knew it was open. The industry's own consultants describe the appeal plainly: three to four months to get through the general permit, eight to twelve for an individual one.
I'm not calling any of that a scandal. General permits exist because it would be absurd to run a full public review for every culvert and every backyard dock, and that's a reasonable judgment. But the whole design rests on an assumption, which is that the activities inside a category are small and scattered and add up to very little.
That assumption was written for a different world than the one where a single industry builds the same enormous thing in county after county, on the same five-year cycle the permits themselves run on. And the public notice you have in front of you right now, on this project, exists only because this one was too big to fit through the door.
Remember that the next time somebody proposes to widen the door.
**THE FLOOR**
I don't support a federal moratorium. I've said as much publicly.
A moratorium is a decision to have this fight later, with less leverage, after the money has moved and the land is already zoned. Chesterfield is the proof. The county did eventually tighten its rules. Data centers can no longer be built there by right, and new ones need a conditional use permit and a public hearing. That's real. But it arrived after all three Google campuses had already been approved under the old rules. A new rule that shows up after the land is zoned protects the next project. It does nothing for the one already in the pipeline.
**What I want is a floor. A federal minimum that every locality can build on top of, and that no locality can be pushed below.**
A county-by-county standard is a menu, not a floor. Turned down in Hanover, go to New Kent. Turned down in New Kent, go to Charles City. Turned down in Virginia, go to Georgia.
Every board of supervisors understands that math, and so does everybody sitting across the table from them. Saying no doesn't stop a project. It moves it one county over and takes the tax base with it. That's what makes "yes" feel like the only real option, and it's why the answer has to come from a level of government the project can't drive past.
On water, here are the four minimums I would push for:
**Report it.** Public disclosure of the water source, the peak-day draw, and annual consumption for every large facility. If you're one of the biggest water users in a county, that number belongs to the public.
**Protect stressed aquifers.** No new evaporative cooling drawing from a groundwater system that is already declining or vulnerable to salt water. Eastern Virginia is both.
**Make "closed loop" mean something.** Any company making that claim has to say which loop (the servers, the building, or the whole campus) and disclose how much water evaporates. Right now that phrase is doing an enormous amount of work it hasn't earned.
**Know what 's in the ground before the land gets zoned, where public money is involved.** When state or federal dollars help get a site ready for development, the wetland and stream surveys and a projected water demand number belong on the public record before the rezoning vote. Not three years later in a federal file most residents will never see.
This is going to sound like Washington overruling a county. It isn't. Nobody in Congress should be telling a board of supervisors how to vote on a rezoning, and I would be skeptical of any bill that did. The zoning decision stays exactly where it belongs, with the people your neighbors elected, in a room your neighbors can walk into.
This is a disclosure requirement attached to public funding, and that's a normal thing. Public money already comes with conditions on reporting and accounting. If taxpayers are helping pay to make a site development-ready, taxpayers ought to know what's on that ground before the vote instead of after it. Chesterfield received $38 million in state site-readiness grants for the Upper Magnolia property. The principle is the same whichever level of government writes the check: more information going to local voices, not less authority for them.
**WHAT I 'LL DO**
**Introduce that floor as legislation in my first session,** including all four standards above.
**Close the groundwater gap.** Federal notice and comment rights for large industrial groundwater withdrawals in designated stressed aquifers, so the Northern Neck has the same standing Chesterfield has today.
To be specific about who that covers, because I don't want anybody to guess. This is aimed at industrial users pulling hundreds of thousands of gallons a day. It does not touch a household well. It does not touch a farm well, an irrigation permit, or a livestock operation. I would write that exclusion into the bill in plain language, and I'd want it there before anybody voted on it.
Farmers are not the problem here. Farmers are a large part of why I care about this in the first place. If the aquifer under the Northern Neck starts taking on salt, the families growing corn and soybeans on ground their grandfathers cleared lose first and lose worst, and drilling deeper is expensive and only buys time.
The watermen lose on the other end of the same problem. Every acre of wetland filled upstream is filtration the Bay doesn't get, and sediment and nitrogen that end up in the rivers they work. The two halves of this are the same fight.
**Defend the public notice.** Fewer comment periods and shorter windows is not efficiency. It is the removal of the last place ordinary people can have a say in how these projects land on them.
**Quarterly field hearings in this district,** on the record, in Reedville, Gloucester, Williamsburg, and Midlothian, with residents as the witnesses and the transcript published.
**THE PART THAT 'S ON YOU**
I find this hopeful, and I don't say that lightly.
This is still winnable. Hanover voted a data center down 4 to 3. Three votes the other way and it gets approved. The difference was residents who showed up, spoke on the record, and made it politically impossible to look away.
And right now there's a five-minute version of that available to you.
The Army Corps comment period on Project Skye (Docket NAO-2026-00282, Norfolk District) closes Tuesday, July 28. Deep Creek. Eighteen acres of forested wetland and a mile and a half of stream.
Last week, six hundred Chesterfield residents went to Google's open houses and asked how much water it would take, how much power, and what happens to Deep Creek. Not one word anybody said that night exists in any official record.
What you write to the Corps does.
Ask for a hearing, and say why. Put it in your own words. A hundred letters saying the same thing in a hundred different ways is worth more than a hundred copies of mine.
These are the things I'd raise, and I'd like them raised by more people than me:
• **The missing page.** Every sheet of the impact drawings points to a table on the final page. That page isn't in the file the public was given. Nobody outside the applicant can check a single number in this permit. Say so.
• **The timing.** On July 23, 2026 the state told the applicant its submission wasn't complete and paused its review. Ask why the public's deadline is Tuesday when the file isn't finished.
• **The whole buildout, not one parcel.** A road corridor, transmission work, and another campus are drawn on Google's own exhibits and left out of this permit's math. Ask for them to be counted together.
• **The water numbers,** in writing, before any permit issues.
• **The historic properties review,** finished before the decision instead of after.

Data centers put pressure on Virginia's water three different ways in three different places, which is exactly why we keep losing these fights, one county at a time. | | | Jul 27 | | | | | | | | | | | | There's a federal comment window on 887 acres in Chesterfield that closes tomorrow (July 28th). You 're receiving this because you signed up for updates from Jason Knapp's campaign for Congress in VA-01. This is our home for longer writing. Unsubscribe anytime below. Thanks for reading Jason Knapp! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. The short version The Army Corps of Engineers is taking public comments on Google's , an 887-acre data center campus in Chesterfield County. The permit would fill in, permanently erasing, about 18 acres of forested wetland and a mile and a half of stream. Comments close TOMORROW, Tuesday, July 28. Docket NAO-2026-00282. Why write. This is the only point in the entire approval where somebody is legally required to take what you say, put it in a permanent public record, and answer it. The rezoning happened four years ago. The land was sold last summer. Six hundred people asked questions at Google's open houses recently and not one word of it was written down anywhere as part of any official record. This is different, and nothing here has been decided yet. Ask for a public hearing. Any person can, in writing, during the comment period. The Corps has to grant it unless it finds the issues raised are insubstantial. That's a low bar, and whether it gets cleared comes down to how many people raise something real. Four things worth raising: 1. The impacts table isn 't in the public file. There are drawings and information contained within ten sheets. Nine were published. Every one of those nine drawings points to a table on the tenth. Strangely, nobody outside the applicant can check a single number in this permit. 2. The state paused its review on July 23, 2026 because the application wasn't complete. The public's deadline is five days after that. 3. Almost all of the stream being filled is headwater channel. The wide corridors at the edges of the property are left alone. What gets filled are the small draws at the top of the system, and those are the ones doing the flood storage and filtration work. 4. The rest of the buildout isn 't counted. A road corridor, transmission work, and another campus are drawn on Google's own exhibits and left out of this permit's math. How to comment, three ways: • Our step-by-step walkthrough: • Direct to the Corps: • By email: CENAO.REGROD@usace.army.mil (put NAO-2026-00282 in the subject line) The public notice and drawings are . It takes about five minutes. You don't have to live in Chesterfield, you don't have to live in Virginia, and you don't have to be an expert. You need to be a concerned citizen in this country. If you are reading this, that is likely, you. A note before you start. This runs long. The important part is above, and I hope you'll file. The rest is here because the process is the story. What's happening on Deep Creek is running in other counties right now, same steps, same order. Knowing the outcome won't help you with the next one. Knowing how the decision gets made lets you explain it to a neighbor over a fence, and tells you which things are worth saying to a federal agency. If five minutes is all you've got, the box above is the whole ask. I put water ahead of the power side of this on purpose. (That piece, who pays to build the grid and why your bill keeps climbing, goes out later.) Power problems are expensive, and expensive problems can be fixed. You can build generation. You can rewrite a rate structure. You can move a cost from one column to another. But a wetland that gets filled in does not come back, and an aquifer that takes on salt water does not come back. Not in our lifetimes, and not in our grandchildren's. Money is recoverable. Water, in the two forms I'm about to describe, is not. I learned how to think about water at sea, where the accounting is straightforward. On a ship, you make your own water. Evaporators run around the clock turning seawater into fresh, and every gallon in the tank is accounted for. When the evaporators go down, you go to what we call "water hours". Here's the thing about water hours. The engineer knows the exact number of gallons left. The kid on the third deck doesn't know the number, and doesn't need to. He knows his shower just went from five minutes to one, and he knows exactly why. Nobody has to explain it to him. Nobody pretends it isn't happening. Virginia is approving some of the largest industrial water users in the Commonwealth's history right now. Most people have no idea it's happening, and almost nobody can tell you the number. That's the part I want to fix. But before we can, we have to be clear about what's actually being argued over, because it isn't one thing. THREE PROBLEMS, NOT ONE I hear this at candidate forums, at meet-and-greets, at supervisor meetings, sitting with watermen down on the water and with farmers whose families have worked the same ground for generations. Everybody says "the water issue" like it's one thing. It isn't. Data centers put pressure on Virginia's water in three different ways, and where you live determines which one is coming for you. In Northern Virginia, the problem is how much they take out. Loudoun County draws its water from the Potomac River and Goose Creek, and that supply is backstopped by reservoirs upstream in Maryland, Virginia, and West Virginia. The county also built about twenty miles of pipeline to send treated wastewater to data centers for cooling instead of drinking water (roughly 736 million gallons of it in 2024). Even with all that, Northern Virginia's data centers used close to two billion gallons in 2023, up 63 percent from 2019. That's a real strain on a river. But a river refills. Next spring's rain puts it back. In the Richmond corridor, the problem is what gets destroyed. This one isn't about pumping at all. It's about filling in the wetlands and streams that hold, cool, and clean the water in the first place, and putting a building on top of them. Once that's done, it doesn't matter how efficient the cooling system is. What was lost is lost. On the Northern Neck and the Middle Peninsula, the problem is that we can 't get it back. No big river intake. No reservoir agreement. What we have is deep groundwater that is already declining and already at risk of turning salty. Three different mechanisms. One industry. And because each county only ever sees its own version of it, every county fights this alone, and none of them can see that they're all up against the same playbook. That is the whole argument for a federal floor, and I'll come back to it. WHAT 'S HAPPENING RIGHT NOW: 887 ACRES ON DEEP CREEK Google has three data center campuses planned in Chesterfield County. The largest is called Project Skye. It's 887.7 acres in the Upper Magnolia Green area: five data center buildings and three substations, south of Genito Road and east of Moseley Road.1 The federal permit application is a public document, and you can read the whole thing yourself at the link above. Start with the names , because the one on the permit and the one on the ground aren't quite the same. Google's own project site says the property is bounded to the south by the corridor of Horsepen Creek.2 Otterdale Branch runs along the north. Those two feed Deep Creek, which runs to the Appomattox and then the James. Chesterfield opened a $100 million middle school named after Deep Creek last July, a mile and a half from here. The permit would permanently fill 17.99 acres of forested wetlands and 8,115 feet of stream channel. A mile and a half of creek. It would also convert another 7.23 acres of forested wetland into emergent wetland, which means the trees come out and what's left behind is marsh.3 Surveys of the property found 147 acres of wetlands and about six miles of streams on it altogether.4 The proposal fills about 18 of those 147 acres and a mile and a half of those six miles. Twelve percent of the wetland. A quarter of the stream. Put that way it sounds like most of it survives. Which part survives matters more than how much. Picture the creek network on that property as a tree lying on its side. The main channel is the trunk. Branching off it are smaller and smaller draws, and out at the ends are the shallow ones that only run water after a rain. The plan keeps the trunk. Those wide corridors along the south and east edges of the property aren't touched. Two of the ten drawing sheets cover that ground and have almost nothing marked on them.5 What gets filled are the branches and the twigs. Small draws threading up between the buildings and the equipment yards. Nearly every foot of the smallest channels on the property is in the fill. That's backwards from how the system works. Water doesn't start in the main channel. It comes off the land into the small stuff first, and that's where most of the slowing and the filtering happens. Fill in the twigs and the trunk is still there, same name on the map. It's just getting raw, fast, unfiltered water now instead of what those small channels used to hand it. Who decides which streams count. There's a line in this process between a stream that gets a protective buffer and one that doesn't, and it comes down to how often water runs in it. Perennial channels, a channel that carries flowing water year round in a normal year, sustained between rain events by groundwater discharge, get a buffer under Virginia's Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act. The smaller ones mostly don't. So somebody has to label them. Every channel on that property gets called perennial, intermittent, or ephemeral, and the label is what determines whether it's protected[[1]](). The labeling was done by the applicant's consultant, who walked each channel and scored it. On May 8, 2026 the state issued its determination letter for this property. It confirms where the water is. It does not confirm the labels. The letter says it outright: the approval doesn't include stream type. So to me it would appear that the labels came from the applicant, the labels set the buffer line, and as far as we can tell, no agency has checked the labels. To be clear, we are not saying that anyone or any agency "cooked the numbers". The scoring followed the standard method and the scores weren't close to the line. The Corps sent a biologist to walk the property in April, and she caught a mapping error the consultant had to fix. That's the system working. She had the field data and the full drawing set. You and I have nine sheets of a set of ten. The impact drawings run ten sheets. Nine were published. All nine points to an impacts table on the tenth, and the tenth isn't there, available for public review. That table is the only document that says which channel, how many feet, and where. The notice says 8,115 feet of stream get filled. The February application, the newest file the public can reach, says 7,964. The 150-foot gap isn't the point. The point is that a total is all anyone outside the applicant can see, and totals move for reasons you can't audit when you cannot fully see how that total was calculated. After the April walk, one channel was reclassified, one shrank, and one came off the map entirely. A channel that carried a fill number in February is gone from the next inventory. So ask for the tenth sheet. Not because 150 feet decides anything, but because you're being asked to weigh in on the size of this by Tuesday, using the only file you're allowed to open, and it isn't the one the agency is using. Why a wetland matters, in broad and plain terms. A forested wetland isn't scenery. It's working infrastructure that the public never had to pay for. It soaks up stormwater during heavy rains and lets it out slowly over the following days, which is what keeps the creek from tearing out its own banks and keeps the road downstream from going under. It filters sediment and nitrogen out of the runoff before that water reaches the James River and, eventually, the Chesapeake Bay. And a wooded wetland does that job considerably better than a grassy one, because the trees, the deep root systems, and a century of leaf litter in the soil are doing most of the work. That's why converting seven acres from forest to marsh is a real loss even though a map would still label it "wetland." What mitigation credits do, and what they don 't. To compensate for the loss, Google proposes to buy 43.31 wetland credits and 9,213 stream credits from approved mitigation banks.9 A mitigation bank is a large wetland that somebody has restored or permanently protected in another location, and credits from it are sold to developers who are filling wetlands elsewhere. Prior to mitigation banks, a developer filling wetlands would promise to build a small replacement nearby, and an enormous number of those failed. Five acres here, three acres there, nobody funding the upkeep, nobody checking back in ten years. Banking pools those obligations into large restoration sites that are professionally managed, legally protected in perpetuity, and finished before the damage is done rather than promised afterward. Measured across an entire watershed or an entire state, that usually produces a better result for the environment than what came before it. It certainly isn't perfect, and there are shortcomings, but it is largely a step forward from past practices. The limitation is the one that matters if you live here. The benefit a wetland provides is local. The flood storage protects the road just below it, not a road forty miles away. The filtering cleans the water in that particular creek. So, when the replacement acres are established in a different watershed (for the neighboring Project Loch campus, the proposed preservation sits in the South Anna River watershed, on the far side of Richmond), the ledger balances, but the geography doesn't. The Chesapeake Bay may come out closer to even. Deep Creek does not. In my view, this means that the trade gets made at one level but the consequences land at another. A company, a mitigation bank, and a federal agency settle it in acres and credits. The family whose road goes under when Deep Creek can no longer hold heavy rains was never a party to that transaction. They had no seat at it and no vote in it, and they pay for it in the only currency they've got, which is their own daily life. Nobody who lives on Deep Creek gets a wetland back. Now look at the legend on those drawings. It includes layers for a road permitted by others, for future Dominion development, and for a transmission easement. Google's own site plan, dated this month, labels that road corridor the future Powhite Parkway extension, alongside a Mount Hermon Road extension, a Westerleigh Parkway extension, and the location of another technology campus.10 Their site also says they'll design and pay for a public sewer main running along Horsepen Creek, the one corridor this permit leaves alone. All of that is drawn on the applicant's own exhibits. None of it is counted in this permit's impact math. Each piece gets reviewed by itself, if it gets reviewed at all, and the total never appears in one place. The historic properties review in that federal file is still open, and the notice specifically invites public comment on it. On species, the Corps finished its consultation on listed bat species in June. The monarch butterfly is proposed for listing and isn't covered by the determination the Corps used.11 The timing matters too. On June 26, three days before the Corps opened this comment period, Virginia DEQ sent the applicant another round of questions on the same submittal. The applicant answered July 10. On July 23, DEQ said that answer wasn't complete and paused its review.12 The state's file is still being assembled, and the federal comment window closes first. None of this is decided. That's the whole point of what comes next. HOW THAT LAND GOT TO THIS POINT This is the part I'd ask you to sit with, because it 's a pattern and not an accident. The Skye property was rezoned in May 2022, when the Chesterfield Board of Supervisors approved 1,728 acres at Upper Magnolia Green for a technology park. That vote was 3 to 2. Two supervisors asked to hold it over for more work, lost that motion, and then voted no. It was rezoned again in May 2025, when the county's Economic Development Authority moved about 980 more acres, with roughly 870 of those restricted to data center use. At the time, the filing referred only to a confidential economic development project. Google was not named publicly. The land sold in July 2025 for nearly $60 million. And the federal wetlands review, the first time anyone publicly counted the 147 acres of wetlands and six miles of stream on that ground, is happening now, in 2026. Read those four dates in order. Zoned. Zoned again. Sold. Surveyed. The survey came last. So, when the supervisors voted, and when the land changed hands for nearly $60 million, there was no public document saying how much wetland or how much stream was on that property. Nobody in that room had the number, because the number didn't exist yet. The public got two turns to speak, and both of them landed off by a step. At the rezoning, residents could argue about whether data centers belonged out there. What nobody could tell them was what it would cost the creeks, because nobody had counted the creeks yet. Now they can comment on the creeks. The zoning is finished and the land has changed hands. Both times, the information you'd need to answer the question was on the other side of the decision. Nobody broke a rule here, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Every step in that sequence was legal, and most of it happened in open meetings. That's exactly why it's worth talking about. The sequence itself is the problem, and the same sequence is running in county after county. Chesterfield has since changed its ordinance. Data centers there can no longer be built by right; a new one now requires a conditional use permit and a public hearing. That's a genuine improvement and the county and its Supervisors deserve credit for it. All three Google sites had already been approved under the old rules. That's why rezoning applications across this district are moving at the speed they are. Forty-six data center bills were carried over from this year's General Assembly session into 2027. Everyone in this business can read a legislative calendar. Get the land entitled now, and whatever Richmond writes next year applies to the next company, not to the parcel you have already locked down. Speed is a strategy. And look at who it's being run against. A county board of supervisors is five people. In most of our counties it's a part-time job with a small stipend. The people holding those seats are farmers, small business owners, retired teachers, a nurse, somebody who runs a marina. They meet at night, after their regular work. They have a county attorney, and a planning staff you could fit in a pickup truck. On the other side of the table is a team of land use attorneys, hydrologists, transmission engineers, and site selection consultants who have run this exact process in a hundred counties and will run it in a hundred more. We are asking those five neighbors of ours to become working experts in wetland delineation and aquifer science, at a night meeting, in three-minute increments, while they're also trying to close a budget gap and maybe trying to figure out how to afford to replace a high school roof. That is not a fair fight. And when it goes badly, it is not their failure. It's the failure of every level of government above them that refused to set a standard they could stand on. WHAT 'S COMING FOR US: THE MISTAKE YOU CAN'T UNDO Now the Northern Neck. I'll say plainly that this part is personal for me. Our family home is in Reedville, and the water I'm about to describe is the water under my own house and my neighbors' houses. Most of eastern Virginia (the Northern Neck, the Middle Peninsula, everything east of I-95) sits inside what the state calls the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area. There is no big river intake out here and no reservoir agreement. What we have is deep groundwater: the Potomac Aquifer, which supplies about 70 percent of everything withdrawn in that management area, and the Piney Point aquifer, which the Northern Neck and Middle Peninsula draw from directly. It is already in trouble. Water levels in parts of the system have dropped by as much as 200 feet. A study by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ, the state agency that regulates water withdrawals) found that average levels in the Potomac Aquifer have been falling since 2021. The state is now steering localities away from it; Caroline County is being pushed toward taking water from the Rappahannock River instead. Hold these two facts side by side. The Commonwealth is telling counties out here to get off the aquifer. And this industry is moving south down I-95 and east along I-64, looking for the next county willing to zone for it. Our version is worse, and this is the mechanism. When you pump hard on a coastal aquifer, you don't just lower the water level. You change the direction the water moves underground. Groundwater here used to flow generally east, toward the coast. Decades of heavy pumping have reversed that, pulling water inland toward the wells and downward into the deepest layers. The boundary between fresh water and saltwater moves right along with it. The places most at risk are the ones closest to salt water, and the Northern Neck is a peninsula with the Chesapeake Bay on one side, the Potomac on the other, and the Rappahannock underneath. There's a second effect on top of that one. As an aquifer loses pressure, the ground above it compacts and settles. The Virginia coastal plain is sinking about one to three millimeters a year and combined with rising seas that produces five to eight millimeters of change annually in some places. Deeper wells, higher water, more flooding. All from the same cause. An over-drawn river refills. An aquifer that goes salty does not. Not in your lifetime and not in your grandchildren's. Northern Virginia's water mistakes are expensive. Ours would be permanent. And this ought to bother everybody out here. Inside a groundwater management area, you need a state permit to withdraw 300,000 gallons or more in a month.13 Household wells fall well below that and aren't reported at all. So, the families with the most to lose, everyone on a private well from Reedville to Deltaville to Lanexa, don't appear anywhere in the state's data. If your well turns brackish, there is no state record that it ever existed. ONE ROOM WHERE YOU COUNT, AND ONE WHERE YOU DON 'T Here is the gap that made me want to write this. When a project fills in wetlands or streams, it needs a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. And that permit comes with something almost nothing else has in this whole process: a legal obligation to hear from you. The Corps publishes public notices and opens a comment period. Every comment becomes part of the official record, and that record is public. The Corps uses those comments to evaluate the project's impacts, to prepare its environmental review, and to weigh what the regulation calls the public interest. That list specifically includes water quality, water supply and conservation, flood hazards, and, in the actual words of the rule, the needs and welfare of the people.14 The evaluation is required to account for cumulative impacts, not this one project in isolation. And here's the part most people have never been told. Any person can request a public hearing in writing during the comment period. In the Corps' own language in this very notice: requests for a public hearing will be granted, unless the District Engineer determines that the issues raised are insubstantial or there is otherwise no valid interest to be served by a hearing.15 Not "may consider." Granted. And if they say no, they have to say why. Be precise about what's up for decision here, because it changes what's worth writing. The comment period isn't in question. It's running right now and it closes on Tuesday, July 28th. What hasn't been decided is the hearing. The test isn't whether your comment is persuasive or well written. Read the standard again. The hearing happens unless the issues raised are insubstantial. That is a low bar, and it is the only bar, and it turns entirely on what people put in the file. Set that against everything else in this process. A company can hold an open house where not one word said by a resident is written down anywhere. A county can adopt an overlay district that replaces public hearings with staff-level permits. A utility rate case can move through a commission most people have never heard of. But if a project fills waters of the United States, a federal agency has to put your objection in the file and answer for it. Some people will call that a technicality. I call it one of the last pieces of working democratic machinery left in this process, and it does not belong to environmental lawyers or to anybody's side. It belongs to whoever shows up. That is true here, it is true across Virginia, and it is true in every county in this country where people are about to have a decision handed to them that they never got a vote on. Now the room where you don't count. Section 404 covers filling in water. It does not cover pumping water out. That one distinction changes what your objection is worth. If a company wants to bulldoze a stream, a federal agency must publish a notice, take your comment, and grant you a hearing unless it finds your concerns insubstantial. If that same company wants to pump a million gallons a day out of the aquifer under your house, there's no federal notice at all. It's a state permit. Virginia does publish notice and take comment on those, and I want to be fair about that. But the hearing standard is different. At the state level a hearing may be held if the response is significant and there are substantial disputed issues.16 Federally it must be held unless someone finds the opposite. One is a presumption in your favor. The other is somebody's discretion. And for the water that matters most out here, we get the second one. That gap didn't get there by accident, and Congress is the only place it can be closed. A caveat, because I don't want to oversell what you've got here. Project Skye gets an individual permit and a public notice because it's enormous. Most projects don't. The Clean Water Act also lets the Corps write general permits, which pre-authorize whole categories of work that the agency has determined will have no more than minimal effects. If your project fits inside a category, you don't get a public notice. You file a short notification, or sometimes nothing at all, and you go. That's not a small side door. The nationwide permit program authorizes roughly 25,000 reported activities a year, plus about 30,000 more that don't require reporting at all.17 Against that, the individual permits that generate a notice like this one are a rounding error. Now the part that should stop you. The Corps reissued the nationwide permits this past January, effective in March and running through 2031.18 In that reissuance, the permit covering commercial development was modified to name data centers explicitly, including, in the Corps' own words, artificial intelligence and machine learning facilities.19 The category now has this industry's name written into it. The limits are real. Half an acre of wetland loss, 300 feet of streambed. Skye is thirty-six times over that, which is exactly why we're getting a comment period. But look at how the streambed limit works: a district engineer can waive the 300 feet for intermittent and ephemeral channels by writing a determination that the effects are minimal.20 There it is again. The same line between a stream that counts and one that mostly doesn't, doing the same work, in a different rule. Virginia adds a layer. The nationwide permit for commercial development is suspended here, replaced by a state programmatic general permit that the Corps and DEQ run together. The current one expires August 1st and a new five-year version takes its place the same day.21 The public comment period on that reissuance ran last fall and closed in October. Almost nobody knew it was open. The industry's own consultants describe the appeal plainly: three to four months to get through the general permit, eight to twelve for an individual one. I'm not calling any of that a scandal. General permits exist because it would be absurd to run a full public review for every culvert and every backyard dock, and that's a reasonable judgment. But the whole design rests on an assumption, which is that the activities inside a category are small and scattered and add up to very little. That assumption was written for a different world than the one where a single industry builds the same enormous thing in county after county, on the same five-year cycle the permits themselves run on. And the public notice you have in front of you right now, on this project, exists only because this one was too big to fit through the door. Remember that the next time somebody proposes to widen the door. THE FLOOR I don't support a federal moratorium. I've said as much publicly. A moratorium is a decision to have this fight later, with less leverage, after the money has moved and the land is already zoned. Chesterfield is the proof. The county did eventually tighten its rules. Data centers can no longer be built there by right, and new ones need a conditional use permit and a public hearing. That's real. But it arrived after all three Google campuses had already been approved under the old rules. A new rule that shows up after the land is zoned protects the next project. It does nothing for the one already in the pipeline. What I want is a floor. A federal minimum that every locality can build on top of, and that no locality can be pushed below. A county-by-county standard is a menu, not a floor. Turned down in Hanover, go to New Kent. Turned down in New Kent, go to Charles City. Turned down in Virginia, go to Georgia. Every board of supervisors understands that math, and so does everybody sitting across the table from them. Saying no doesn't stop a project. It moves it one county over and takes the tax base with it. That's what makes "yes" feel like the only real option, and it's why the answer has to come from a level of government the project can't drive past. On water, here are the four minimums I would push for: Report it. Public disclosure of the water source, the peak-day draw, and annual consumption for every large facility. If you're one of the biggest water users in a county, that number belongs to the public. Protect stressed aquifers. No new evaporative cooling drawing from a groundwater system that is already declining or vulnerable to salt water. Eastern Virginia is both. Make "closed loop" mean something. Any company making that claim has to say which loop (the servers, the building, or the whole campus) and disclose how much water evaporates. Right now that phrase is doing an enormous amount of work it hasn't earned. Know what 's in the ground before the land gets zoned, where public money is involved. When state or federal dollars help get a site ready for development, the wetland and stream surveys and a projected water demand number belong on the public record before the rezoning vote. Not three years later in a federal file most residents will never see. This is going to sound like Washington overruling a county. It isn't. Nobody in Congress should be telling a board of supervisors how to vote on a rezoning, and I would be skeptical of any bill that did. The zoning decision stays exactly where it belongs, with the people your neighbors elected, in a room your neighbors can walk into. This is a disclosure requirement attached to public funding, and that's a normal thing. Public money already comes with conditions on reporting and accounting. If taxpayers are helping pay to make a site development-ready, taxpayers ought to know what's on that ground before the vote instead of after it. Chesterfield received $38 million in state site-readiness grants for the Upper Magnolia property. The principle is the same whichever level of government writes the check: more information going to local voices, not less authority for them. WHAT I 'LL DO Introduce that floor as legislation in my first session, including all four standards above. Close the groundwater gap. Federal notice and comment rights for large industrial groundwater withdrawals in designated stressed aquifers, so the Northern Neck has the same standing Chesterfield has today. To be specific about who that covers, because I don't want anybody to guess. This is aimed at industrial users pulling hundreds of thousands of gallons a day. It does not touch a household well. It does not touch a farm well, an irrigation permit, or a livestock operation. I would write that exclusion into the bill in plain language, and I'd want it there before anybody voted on it. Farmers are not the problem here. Farmers are a large part of why I care about this in the first place. If the aquifer under the Northern Neck starts taking on salt, the families growing corn and soybeans on ground their grandfathers cleared lose first and lose worst, and drilling deeper is expensive and only buys time. The watermen lose on the other end of the same problem. Every acre of wetland filled upstream is filtration the Bay doesn't get, and sediment and nitrogen that end up in the rivers they work. The two halves of this are the same fight. Defend the public notice. Fewer comment periods and shorter windows is not efficiency. It is the removal of the last place ordinary people can have a say in how these projects land on them. Quarterly field hearings in this district, on the record, in Reedville, Gloucester, Williamsburg, and Midlothian, with residents as the witnesses and the transcript published. THE PART THAT 'S ON YOU I find this hopeful, and I don't say that lightly. This is still winnable. Hanover voted a data center down 4 to 3. Three votes the other way and it gets approved. The difference was residents who showed up, spoke on the record, and made it politically impossible to look away. And right now there's a five-minute version of that available to you. The Army Corps comment period on Project Skye (Docket NAO-2026-00282, Norfolk District) closes Tuesday, July 28. Deep Creek. Eighteen acres of forested wetland and a mile and a half of stream. Last week, six hundred Chesterfield residents went to Google's open houses and asked how much water it would take, how much power, and what happens to Deep Creek. Not one word anybody said that night exists in any official record. What you write to the Corps does. Ask for a hearing, and say why. Put it in your own words. A hundred letters saying the same thing in a hundred different ways is worth more than a hundred copies of mine. These are the things I'd raise, and I'd like them raised by more people than me: • The missing page. Every sheet of the impact drawings points to a table on the final page. That page isn't in the file the public was given. Nobody outside the applicant can check a single number in this permit. Say so. • The timing. On July 23, 2026 the state told the applicant its submission wasn't complete and paused its review. Ask why the public's deadline is Tuesday when the file isn't finished. • The whole buildout, not one parcel. A road corridor, transmission work, and another campus are drawn on Google's own exhibits and left out of this permit's math. Ask for them to be counted together. • The water numbers, in writing, before any permit issues. • The historic properties review, finished before the decision instead of after. We've posted step-by-step instructions at . It walks you through the Corps' online system, tells you exactly what to reference (Docket NAO-2026-00282), and gives you plain language you can adapt. It takes about five minutes. If you'd rather do it directly, comments go to the Corps' Regulatory Request System at , or by email to CENAO.REGROD@usace.army.mil. The public notice and drawings are . You don't have to live in Chesterfield. You don't have to be an expert, and you don't need to use technical words. You have to be a member of the public with an interest in the waters of the United States. And if you're reading this, you are. Then ask the people who represent you, in both parties, what they've filed and where they've testified. The Democratic primary for VA-01 is August 4. Early voting is open now. About Jason: Jason Knapp grew up in a single-parent household on food stamps and Medicaid, raised by a mother who worked her way out of poverty to become a key contributor on several NASA missions. He went on to serve 21 years as a Naval Officer and F/A-18 pilot, flying combat missions over Iraq. Over his career he held senior legislative and political posts across the national-security world: as a Navy Defense Legislative Fellow in Congress (where he met his wife, who spent most of her career on the Hill), as Deputy Director of Legislative Affairs for U.S. European Command, and as an Executive Officer at NATO, working alongside 28 allied nations. He later worked in economic development siting manufacturing facilities, where power and water availability were the make-or-break variables on every deal. The Knapp family home is in Reedville, Virginia, in the heart of VA-01. Thanks for reading Jason Knapp! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. How this was put together. The permit file for this project runs to several hundred pages: the application and its appendices, the engineering drawings, correspondence between the applicant and two agencies, and the federal and state rules that govern all of it. I used an AI assistant to read through that material, cross-reference it, and help edit what you just read. Every factual claim traces to a primary document, and those documents are listed in the sources below so you can check any of it against the original. The judgments about what matters here, and the decision to publish it, are mine. SOURCES 1. Public Notice NAO-2026-00282; 33 C.F.R. 327.4. 16. Virginia DEQ, water permit public notices and hearing requests. 17. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers nationwide permit program activity counts, 2026 reissuance materials. 18. Reissuance and Modification of Nationwide Permits, 91 Fed. Reg. (Jan. 8, 2026), effective March 15, 2026. 19. Nationwide Permit 39, Commercial and Institutional Developments, 2026 reissuance. 20. Nationwide Permit 39, streambed loss limit and district engineer waiver provision. 21. USACE Norfolk District, proposed reissuance of 26-SPGP-RCIR and 26-SPGP-LT, public notice September 8, 2025, comments due October 8, 2025; current SPGPs expire August 1, 2026. Virginia DEQ, Wetlands and Streams. [[1]]() Perennial. Flows continuously in a typical year. Water table intersects the channel. Supports fish and aquatic insects that need permanent water. Intermittent. Flows seasonally, usually winter and spring, when the water table rises into the channel. Goes dry in late summer and fall. Ephemeral.** Flows only during and shortly after rain or snowmelt. The channel bottom is always above the water table. Most roadside swales and headwater draws are ephemeral. Join us for a Volusia County House Party in support of Marialana Kinter for Congress on Tuesday, July 28th at 5:00 PM at the home of Barbara Grimm, located at 1605 West French Ave., Orange City, FL 32763. This is a great opportunity to meet Marialana, hear her vision for Florida's 7th Congressional District, and learn how you can help build a grassroots campaign that puts working families first.
If you live in Volusia County, we encourage you to bring your friends, neighbors, and family members. Every new supporter helps us expand our movement and reach more voters before Election Day. Parking is available in the grassy area near the home.
Together, we can build the volunteer powered campaign that will win this race. Register today at kinterforcongress.com/events and invite someone to join you. We look forward to seeing you there!
